Maladaptive Strategies.value: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings
Making any plans for the future
I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking

Threat.value: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
When I remember the event I feel intense shame

vignette: Eleanor Vance was thirty-two when a sudden siege turned her hometown into a grid of pulverized concrete. For eleven weeks, she huddled in a damp basement apartment, surviving by tracking the precise rhythm of artillery thuds that vibrated through the floorboards. She had come to believe that danger announced itself only in the moments before impact, a calculus that made the sky and the approach of any heavy vehicle a source of visceral dread. When the shelling finally stopped, she fled north, carrying only a suitcase and the unspoken weight of what she had endured. The trauma was not a single explosion but a prolonged collapse of civilian safety, leaving her with a nervous system permanently calibrated to anticipate structural failure at any moment. In the months that followed, the fragmented images of the basement would surface without warning. Eleanor found it difficult to deliberately recall the event, her mind blocking the narrative while her body retained the taste of grit and the dark press of falling dust. When these nonverbal memories forced their way up, the shame on recall was immediate and suffocating, as if her inability to name the experience made her complicit in her own terror. Rather than endure the confusion, she began to avoid all feelings, turning to long hours of video games and internet scrolling to keep her mind blank. The memories did not stay buried, however. The persistent shame and fragmented recollections inevitably heightened her sense of vulnerability, causing her to scan every room and parking lot for signs of danger. She avoided unfamiliar places because she felt unable to assess the threat, and ordinary strangers approaching her in quiet neighborhoods triggered a physiological alarm so sharp she would drop her keys and step back. Now at seventy-six, retired after a lifelong career as a radiologist, Eleanor's home study serves as both her former workplace and her current sanctuary. The familiar glow of dual monitors once allowed her to diagnose subtle fractures on X-rays, but now it functions as a screen escape. Her decades of reading diagnostic images had conditioned her to expect clinical certainty, but her mind now offered only static. She spends hours navigating medical archives and endless digital feeds, successfully delaying the return of the basement's sensory ghosts. Yet the strategy is inherently fragile. When her focus wavers and the screens go dark, the avoidance fractures, and the hard-to-recall memories resurface with sudden clarity. The shame on recall floods back, pushing her immediately to scan the horizon of her own living room. Her deliberate efforts to avoid all feelings and make future plans left her emotionally exposed, and as the screens faded, the unprocessed dread simply migrated to her environment. She began to scan every unfamiliar place for danger, avoiding streets she couldn't navigate because she couldn't assess the threat, and flinching when strangers approached her in ordinary settings. She has come to believe that making any plans for the future is a reckless gamble, so she has stopped suggesting retirement trips or rearranging her garden. This refusal to look ahead has hardened into a quiet distance in her marriage; her husband waits for her at the dinner table, watching her stare at the television, knowing that her inability to envision tomorrow has slowly erased their shared future. Worse, when she caught herself scanning the garden path for approaching vehicles, the heightened vigilance would trigger a sudden, visceral flashback to the rubble, locking her throat and pulling her mind back to the moment she was cornered. It was this tightening loop that finally brought Eleanor to seek help. The screens no longer quieted the static, and the avoidance had left her isolated in a house that felt perpetually under threat. She came to the clinic fearing that her memories would never stop dictating her days, but she hoped, desperately, to find a way to sit with the shame without drowning in it, to plan a tomorrow that did not require a shelter.
